A content delivery network, or CDN, helps websites load faster by storing copies of content in many different places around the world, instead of keeping everything in just one location. When someone first requests a webpage, video, or image, that request normally has to travel all the way to the origin server, which is the original computer where the content is permanently stored. This can take time, especially if the person is far away. To speed things up, a CDN keeps copies of popular content at an edge location, which is a smaller storage point positioned closer to where people actually are, such as in a nearby city or country. When a request arrives and the nearby edge location already has the needed copy ready to go, that's called a cache hit, meaning the content can be delivered instantly without contacting the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep copies of the most popular books, so readers don't have to travel to one central national library every single time. This system reduces waiting time, eases pressure on the origin server, and keeps things running smoothly even when many people request the same content at once.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the master copy of content | It's the ultimate source, but reaching it directly is slower |
| Edge location | A nearby storage point holding copies of popular content | It shortens the distance content must travel |
| Cache hit | When requested content is already available nearby | It means near-instant delivery with no long-distance trip |
| Content delivery network | A network of edge locations working together globally | It keeps websites fast and reliable for everyone, everywhere |
